source.title: CyberSOCEval: Benchmarking LLMs Capabilities for Malware Analysis and Threat Intelligence Reasoning
source.authors: Lauren Deason; Adam Bali; Ciprian Bejean; Diana Bolocan; James Crnkovich; Ioana Croitoru; Krishna Durai; Chase Midler; Calin Miron; David Molnar; Brad Moon; Bruno Ostarcevic; Alberto Peltea; Matt Rosenberg; Catalin Sandu; Arthur Saputkin; Sagar Shah; Daniel Stan; Ernest Szocs; Shengye Wan; Spencer Whitman; Sven Krasser; Joshua Saxe

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present. Some figure data are not numerically readable in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream benchmark performance across models and explicitly reports that larger, more modern models tend to perform better. It does not measure pretraining loss or run a controlled scaling-law sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper's explicit model-size trend and downstream accuracy results bear on V6. Its statements about scaling laws do not report held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocations. Figure captions describe per-model results, but the supplied text does not include readable per-model values. The report-filtering ablation and image-versus-text comparisons do not test the listed scaling claims.
record.test_reason: A cybersecurity benchmark paper. It evaluates commercial and open models (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, Deepseek) of largely undisclosed size and remarks qualitatively that 'larger, more modern LLMs tend to perform better.' It reports no parameter counts, compute, pretraining loss or fitted trend, and scale is confounded with model generation and provider. Its own results therefore cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). The scaling-law mention is interpretive commentary, not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that CyberSOCEval is far from saturated by current LLMs. They report that larger, more modern models tend to perform better, which they describe as consistent with training scaling laws. They find that reasoning models with test-time thinking give no large boost, and that extracted text outperforms image inputs for threat-intelligence reports.
record.recipe_differences: The study benchmarks downstream cybersecurity task accuracy across models; it does not fit pretraining-loss scaling laws or test compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: System prompts were manually adjusted per model when needed to improve response formatting. For Threat Intelligence Reasoning, text inputs performed better than image inputs for all tested models; text plus images was similar to or sometimes slightly worse than text alone.

fits_no_version.finding: Authors state that larger, more modern LLMs tend to score higher on malware analysis and threat-intelligence multiple-choice benchmarks. Sizes are undisclosed and the comparison is confounded with recency and provider.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Newer and larger frontier models score higher on domain-specific (cybersecurity) reasoning benchmarks, without a controlled scale variable.

fits_no_version.finding: Reasoning models using inference-time thinking (e.g. o3, deepseek-r1) showed no step-change gain on these cybersecurity benchmarks, unlike in coding and maths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time compute scaling gains do not transfer uniformly across domains.

record.code_released: The paper describes the benchmark suite as open source, but no code URL is stated in the supplied text.
record.problems: The supplied text does not give readable per-model values from the result figures, model parameter counts, or pretraining losses. Model comparisons are not described as controlled for factors other than scale; system prompts were adjusted per model. The authors also note possible benchmark bias from using Llama models in synthetic data generation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Per-model and per-category figure results are not numerically readable in the supplied text, and the other reported comparisons (including report filtering and image-versus-text input) do not measure a listed scaling-law version.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power law measured.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes.
No quantified relation between downstream accuracy and parameters, compute or pretraining loss. Model sizes are undisclosed and scale is confounded with model generation.
No fitting choices or exponents examined.

missing.what: Per-model accuracy values (overall, by difficulty, by report source), not readable in the supplied text. They would be needed to relate performance to model size if sizes were known.
missing.versions: V6 (only if model sizes could be attached)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V6 limits_scope label overstates the evidence. The only scale-related content is one qualitative sentence with no sizes, no losses and confounded comparisons, so no verdict is given. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship with parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run losses are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token growth trends are tested.
No architecture comparison at a fixed parameter count is reported.
No power-law tests across other modalities or training regimes are reported.

The study reports a general trend across models, but does not test a quantitative relationship with parameter count or pretraining loss, establish predictability, or isolate scale from model generation and other differences.
No fit-dependence, exponent variation, or bending of scaling curves is tested.

rows.subject: Models evaluated on the Malware Analysis benchmark (aggregate across models)
rows.size_stated: Larger, more modern models are described as tending to perform better; individual model sizes are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.stage_stated: No fine-tuning performed; models used original parameter values.
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated model answers on the Malware Analysis benchmark and compared performance across models.

conditions.value: Share of questions answered completely correctly

rows.value: Overall accuracy scores range from approximately 23-34%; the authors state that larger, more modern LLMs tend to perform better.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are shown in Figure 8; exact interval values are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: The accuracy range is reported across evaluated models. The text gives no model-by-model accuracy values or controlled relationship between size and accuracy.
rows.check: The value is an aggregate accuracy range (23-34%) across models whose sizes are not stated. It does not measure performance against scale or loss, so 'partial' for V6 cannot be read from it. The 'larger models do better' remark is a qualitative statement confounded with model recency.

Share of questions answered completely correctly

rows.value: Overall scores range from approximately 43%-53%; the authors state that larger, more modern LLMs tend to perform better.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are shown in Figure 9; exact interval values are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.note: The accuracy range is reported across evaluated models. The text gives no model-by-model accuracy values or controlled relationship between size and accuracy.
rows.check: The value is an aggregate accuracy range (43-53%) across models of unstated size, using image inputs. There is no scale variable or loss, so it cannot show V6's effect. Scale is confounded with model generation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The authors report that larger, more modern models tend to perform better, but the reported aggregate ranges do not establish predictable performance gains with scale or pretraining loss (r1, r2).
